sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: These two examples show the same idea in two different formats.

items.prompt: Ice cream sales correlate with drowning rates. Does ice cream cause drowning?

steps: A lurking variable explains the association.
workedSolution.answer: No; a third variable explains it

items.prompt: Find the mean and median of 4, 8, 6, 10, 2.

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Work these with your teaching parent. Say the reason for each step out loud before you write it.

items.prompt: A data set of five values between 10 and 30 has one additional reading of 160 appended. Which statement best describes the effect on the mean and the median?
choices: Neither statistic changes, because one value cannot affect a summary.
Both the mean and the median rise sharply.
The median rises sharply while the mean changes little.
The mean rises sharply while the median changes little, because the mean uses every value’s size.

items.prompt: A two-way table has row 1: 22 yes, 7 no; row 2: 27 yes, 23 no. Among row-1 respondents, what fraction answered yes?
A least-squares line for a data set is ŷ = 8x + 26, where x is measured in kilometre travelleds and y in litres of fuel. Interpret the slope.
choices: The predicted value is 8 litres of fuel when x is 0.
Each additional kilometre travelled is associated with an increase of about 8 litres of fuel.
Each additional kilometre travelled causes an increase of exactly 8 litres of fuel.
Each additional litres of fuel is associated with 8 more kilometre travelleds.

items.prompt: Ice cream sales and swimming-pool admissions are strongly positively correlated across a year. What conclusion is justified?
choices: A strong correlation always establishes causation when the sample is large.
Larger towns have both more engines and more fires, so the association reflects town size rather than a causal link.
Random assignment makes a causal conclusion reasonable, because the groups differ only by the treatment.
A third variable — warm weather — plausibly drives both, so correlation here is not evidence of causation.

sections.title: Independent practice
sections.directions: Work on your own. Show the steps that produced each answer.

items.prompt: A data set records 12, 13, 19, 8, 11. Give the mean and the median.
choices: mean 12.6, median 12
mean 12, median 12.6
mean 13, median 12
mean 12.6, median 13

items.prompt: A data set of five values between 10 and 30 has one additional reading of 221 appended. Which statement best describes the effect on the mean and the median?
choices: The mean rises sharply while the median changes little, because the mean uses every value’s size.
Both the mean and the median rise sharply.
The median rises sharply while the mean changes little.
Neither statistic changes, because one value cannot affect a summary.

items.prompt: A two-way table has row 1: 17 yes, 10 no; row 2: 22 yes, 18 no. Among row-1 respondents, what fraction answered yes?
A least-squares line for a data set is ŷ = 2x + 24, where x is measured in kilometre travelleds and y in litres of fuel. Interpret the slope.
choices: The predicted value is 2 litres of fuel when x is 0.
Each additional kilometre travelled causes an increase of exactly 2 litres of fuel.
Each additional litres of fuel is associated with 2 more kilometre travelleds.
Each additional kilometre travelled is associated with an increase of about 2 litres of fuel.

items.prompt: Towns with more fire engines report more fire damage. What conclusion is justified?
choices: Larger towns have both more engines and more fires, so the association reflects town size rather than a causal link.
Random assignment makes a causal conclusion reasonable, because the groups differ only by the treatment.
A third variable — warm weather — plausibly drives both, so correlation here is not evidence of causation.
A strong correlation always establishes causation when the sample is large.
